chunks: Diode use cases. The question: What are some use cases of a diode?
A diode lets current go one way and not the other, and engineers use that in many ways.
It can turn AC (current that keeps reversing) into DC (current that flows one way), block a battery that is plugged in backwards, or absorb a voltage spike.
A few special diodes do other jobs, such as emitting light. This page asks you to list the uses and say which diode property each one relies on.
Picture a one-way street. You can use it to keep traffic from going the wrong way, as in a rectifier. You can use it to stop a car from backing out, as in battery protection.
And you can give runaway traffic a side road to drain into, as a flyback diode does for a coil. All of those come from one rule: traffic goes one way.
The analogy leaves out the small toll a diode charges in voltage.
Group applications by the property they exploit. In an interview this gives you a structure to work through instead of a random list, and each branch has its own trade-off.
Rectifier: a diode circuit that turns AC into DC. Flyback diode: a diode across a coil that gives its current a safe path when switched off.
Zener diode: a diode designed to conduct in reverse at a set voltage. Forward drop: the voltage lost across a conducting diode, about 0. 7 volts in silicon.
Schottky diode: a diode with a lower forward drop.
Say a user might plug a battery in backwards. Put a diode in series with the supply. Plugged correctly, current flows, and the diode drops about 0. 7 volts.
Plugged backwards, the diode blocks, and the circuit is safe. The price is power: with 2 amps, the diode wastes about 0. 7 volts times 2 amps = 1. 4 watts. That is the whole idea.
"I group diode uses by the property they exploit. One-way conduction gives rectifiers, reverse-polarity protection, OR-ing two supplies, and flyback diodes across inductive loads.
Controlled breakdown gives Zener references and TVS surge clamps, plus the ESD diodes on every IC pin.
And the junction itself makes LEDs, photodiodes, varactors and temperature sensors.
The main cost is the forward drop, so in power paths I'd use a Schottky or an ideal-diode MOSFET."
